title: Introduction
text: Introduction Chicago's zoning code shapes far more than building heights and lot sizes: it determines who can afford to live here, where economic opportunity takes root, and how equitably the city's future growth is shared. This report presents findings from a three-year study by Metropolitan Planning Council, examining how zoning law and regulation have influenced housing availability and affordability, business vitality, and adaptation to climate risks across the city. Grounded in the values of equity, sustainability, and public health, the research draws on an extensive engagement process involving more than 700 individuals from over 450 organizations, including government agencies, community organizations, ward offices, and private sector partners. The findings reveal a city constrained by its own regulatory framework. Just 11% of Chicago is zoned for multifamily housing 1 , while 41% is reserved for the most expensive and land-intensive housing type: detached single-family homes. The consequences of our outdated zoning system are stark and geographically concentrated. For example, 60% of new housing built since 2006 has landed in just five community areas, while 45 of Chicago's 77 community areas have added fewer than 500 new homes in nearly two decades. Meanwhile, Black and Latinx residents have experienced sharp declines in affordability over the last two decades. 60% of the approximately 120,000 new housing units in the city built since 2006 were concentrated in just 5 community areas. Interactive chart redrawn for this site from the figures printed in the source. These disparities extend beyond housing into the economic fabric of neighborhoods. Business concentration follows similar patterns of inequity: majority-white census tracts average 14.7 businesses per 1,000 residents, compared to just 8.6 in majority-Black tracts, a gap tied in part to how zoning allocates space for walkable, pedestrian-oriented commercial corridors. Zoning also has tangible impacts on air, water, and land. Our research shows that Latinx Chicagoans make up 50% of the population in the top fifth most air-polluted areas—and that Latinx neighborhoods tend to have more land zoned for industrial use. These disparities pose both health and economic risks for Chicago’s population. This report argues that hyper-local control, absent a coherent citywide strategy, comes at a real cost to residents' lives. What follows are the key findings and policy recommendations to build a more equitable and thriving Chicago. illustration: Lucie Van der Elst

title: Citywide problems require citywide solutions: A way forward on zoning and land use
text: Citywide problems require citywide solutions: A way forward on zoning and land use Chicago is a city known for what we’ve built—and what we’ve rebuilt. We are renowned for our architecture, our elevated trains, our sweeping public parks, our lakefront skyline, and our people. When the city we had created was destroyed by a historic fire, we marshaled the industry and innovation of the time and built it again. Our story of rebuilding is also one of segregation and harm. Highways carved up our neighborhoods, rampant redlining and exclusionary zoning practices blocked families in Black and Latinx communities from homeownership and wealth building, and polluting industries left some communities with unhealthy air and contaminated land that is still in need of remediation. Just as we have rebuilt our skyline after tragedy, our task now is to rebuild toward a future that addresses the wrongs of our past. We need to craft citywide solutions to citywide problems. We are in a time of skepticism about cities. And the challenges are real: new housing is being built in too few neighborhoods, and the costs of housing continue to rise faster than wages. Too many lots and storefronts are sitting vacant, while small business owners struggle to navigate complicated policies to get businesses off the ground. Across Chicago, all residents are exposed to unhealthy levels of air pollution, and some communities still bear a disproportionate burden. All of these are complex land use questions that the city has a responsibility to tackle. Citywide zoning and land use reforms are a chance to flex our citywide muscle: an opportunity to prove that cities can work, while improving life for all Chicagoans. The recommendations below are informed by MPC and Urban Institute’s stakeholder-guided research, and the perspectives we heard from hundreds of Chicagoans over the course of the Zoning and Land Use Assessment—experts and everyday residents alike. These are reforms that take a citywide approach. We can allow the construction of more homes without project-by-project aldermanic approval, like the two-to-four flats that already fill our neighborhoods but remain illegal to build and rebuild throughout much of the city. We can remove the requirement for new small businesses to navigate expensive zoning relief processes. And we can modernize our zoning to allow areas near transit to evolve into dynamic and walkable places to live and work. The result has been that Chicago is seen as too unpredictable a place to build, housing continues to become more expensive, and segregation continues to divide our city. Aldermanic prerogative—Chicago’s version of hyper-local control—is standing in the way of building a more equitable future for our city. Aldermanic prerogative is a deeply rooted practice here. Through policy and practice, City Council and other government bodies defer to the local alderperson when making decisions about development proposals. Because Chicago’s current zoning and land use policies restrict what’s possible to build “by-right”—under the current zoning rules—many projects can’t advance without the blessing of the local alderperson. This gives alderpersons virtually unquestioned control over what gets built within the boundaries of each of the 50 separate wards. The result has been that Chicago is seen as too unpredictable a place to build, housing continues to become more expensive, and segregation continues to divide our city. Our neighborhoods have different needs, but aldermanic prerogative is not an effective stand-in for neighborhood desires. Each alderperson approaches their role differently. Some have local zoning advisory boards composed of hand-selected residents, local businesses, or local institutions. Some solicit feedback, hold community meetings, or encourage developers to hold meetings. And some do none of these things, negotiating directly with developers. Even when alderpersons receive input from residents, there is no mechanism to check whether this feedback is representative of their constituents, or whether it simply represents those with the time and resources to engage. At the same time, there is also no way to ensure that feedback gets implemented—the power remains the alderperson’s to wield as they wish. The current system pushes our politics toward territorialism and zero-sum thinking. Our challenges are not contained within individual wards, and the solutions are not either. The availability and affordability of new homes, the vibrancy of our business corridors, and the role of industry in our neighborhoods are all citywide issues, and citywide zoning and land use policy could be powerful tools to address them. But for over a century, aldermanic prerogative has prevented this citywide approach, keeping our elected officials locked in political infighting rather than common-sense policymaking. Zoning reform is not a silver bullet. There are generational challenges ahead. Many factors beyond zoning shape our communities, such as public and private investment and disinvestment, community organizations, market incentives, and tax structures. Zoning changes that make room for more homes must be paired with policies that prioritize and incentivize the creation and preservation of homes affordable to the lowest-income Chicagoans. Meanwhile, the unusually large size of City Council for the size of our population, our lack of at-large council members, and our lack of a city charter all fuel our culture of unchecked aldermanic prerogative. And with our piecemeal approach to planning, we lack a way to bring in many voices to conversations about development without getting sidetracked by hyper-local opposition, or piling all of a community’s legitimate needs onto a single development. Zoning reform alone will not solve our city’s fundamental and interrelated problems of resource allocation and governance. Yet zoning reform is a worthwhile citywide project. With zoning and land use reform as a foundation, we can build toward a new Chicago. We can reimagine our policies—zoning and beyond—to build a place where the inequitable outcomes we see reflected in our research no longer persist. We can build a place where families of all incomes can afford a place to live; where all Chicagoans have access to transportation that connects them; where vibrant, livable communities replace empty lots and small businesses can grow without unnecessary barriers; and where everyone can breathe fresh air and drink clean water. To get there, we need a new collaborative and forward-looking status quo that empowers Chicagoans—not ward-by-ward, but across the city. title: Summary: challenges, visions, and policy recommendations
text: Summary: challenges, visions, and policy recommendations THE CHALLENGE THE VISION POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS A worsening affordability crisis is pinching budgets and displacing Chicagoans Make space for more homes that Chicagoans can afford (pp. 10-17) Legalize 4-flats and ADUs citywide: At minimum, allow housing types with up to four units by-right and additional dwelling units (ADUs) in all residential areas. Legalize 6 stories near transit: At minimum, allow apartment buildings with up to 6 stories by-right near rail stations and the most frequent and highest-volume bus lines. Decrease reliance on Planned Developments for multifamily construction: Right-size thresholds for Planned Developments so more multifamily housing can be built by-right. Use zoning tools to promote deep affordability: Prioritize and incentivize affordable housing (fast-track zoning approvals for affordable development, prohibit reactive downzoning, and protect against the loss of naturally affordable units). Jobs and business vitality are inequitably distributed Clear the way for vibrant, livable communities (pp. 18-20) Zone for a dynamic mix of uses near transit: Allow more opportunities for Chicagoans to live, work, and visit places near transit, especially in areas with fewer jobs and/or higher vacancy rates. Expand pedestrian streets near transit: Standardize the use of the pedestrian street designation near transit and modernize pedestrian street eligibility and standards. Bring small-scale business into neighborhoods: Increase the types of businesses allowed in residential neighborhoods, like home-based and small-scale businesses. Too many Chicagoans are exposed to unhealthy pollutants and vulnerable to climate impacts Integrate healthy air, water, and land into zoning and land use practices (pp. 21-26) Update zoning for modern industry: Re-classify manufacturing and industrial uses based on measurable benefits and harms—such as jobs, pollution, environmental impacts, and public health impacts—to encourage low-impact, job-dense industry. Protect overburdened communities from cumulative impacts: Require a holistic review of the expected health and quality-of-life impacts of all proposed intensive industrial facilities. Leverage unbuilt land for permeable surfaces: Use zoning to ensure unbuilt land helps counter flood and heat risk, by requiring or incentivizing permeable surfaces and green infrastructure in setbacks open space , parkways, and parking lots. Target climate-vulnerable areas for mitigation strategies: Prioritize communities most vulnerable to heat and flooding for more green space and remediation. Zoning and land use policy is opaque and difficult to navigate Clarify and streamline zoning process and categories (pp. 27-29) Modernize special uses: Allow most current special use categories by-right, with accompanying use standards. Require Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) review only for uses with likely impacts on health and safety. Reassess other zoning relief categories: Conduct a review of variation and administrative adjustment requests to determine zoning code updates. Centralize information about zoning: Provide a central hub for plain-language materials around zoning standards and processes, prioritizing information that facilitates housing and small business development. Close zoning data gaps: Standardize and publicize data on zoning processes and outcomes. Proactive planning is piecemeal and focused on the neighborhood level Tie zoning to foundational citywide planning and engagement (pp. 30-31) Periodically update zoning to align with a planning vision : Require regular reviews of the zoning code and map based on comprehensive citywide planning that meaningfully engages the public. Improve public input processes: Create a more standardized, transparent, and equitable public input process on land use.

title: What can you expect from this report?
text: What can you expect from this report? In ABOUT THE ZONING AND LAND USE ASSESSMENT , you’ll find an overview of the process MPC went through to produce the research and recommendations contained in this report. In RESEARCH FINDINGS AND POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS , you’ll find a deep dive into MPC’s recommended policies for improving zoning and land use in Chicago. The recommendations, which were developed in consultation with stakeholders, are organized by the challenges they respond to: the worsening housing affordability crisis in Chicago, the inequitable distribution of jobs and business vitality, exposure to pollutants and climate vulnerabilities, an opaque and difficult-to-navigate zoning system, and piecemeal planning practices. In each category, you’ll find the research findings from the Assessment that relate to the challenge, MPC’s specific policy recommendations, additional considerations for policy design and implementation, and example policies from other cities. In CONCLUSION , you’ll find a discussion of the implications of this work. In APPENDIX: ADDITIONAL RESEARCH FINDINGS , you’ll find the research findings from the Assessment that were not included in the body of the report. This includes findings from our analysis of “productive land use” across Chicago neighborhoods; findings on grocery and healthcare availability and zoning; and other findings that did not directly relate to specific policy recommendations but came out of the Assessment’s research focus on seven priority outcomes: affordable housing, strong business corridors, limited pollution exposure, accessible public transit hubs, available groceries and healthcare, mitigation and adaptation to climate change, and productive land use. In APPENDIX: ZONING DISTRICTS , you’ll find an introduction to Chicago’s main zoning designations and their shares of the city’s zoned land area. You’ll also find a (simplified) zoning map of the city. In APPENDIX: RESEARCH METHODOLOGY , you’ll find a detailed account of how the research was conducted, including data sources, assumptions, and research limitations. In APPENDIX: ENGAGEMENT METHODOLOGY , you’ll find a detailed account of how engagement was conducted, including a timeline of engagement across the project, example activities, and how input was documented and synthesized. In ACKNOWLEDGMENTS , you’ll find the team members, partners, funders, and other contributors who made the Assessment possible.

title: About the Zoning and Land Use Assessment
text: About the Zoning and Land Use Assessment What is the Zoning and Land Use Assessment? Reimagining a new citywide status quo for zoning in Chicago requires a shared understanding of the effects our current zoning and land use policies are having on neighborhoods across the city. That’s why MPC—with research support from the Urban Institute—created the Zoning and Land Use Assessment: a collaborative research and engagement initiative designed to explore the impacts of Chicago’s current zoning and land use policies, and propose improvements to better serve public health, equity, and sustainability. Who contributed to the Zoning and Land Use Assessment? The Assessment was a multi-year project that engaged hundreds of stakeholders. Since the project’s launch in 2022, MPC has collaborated with dozens of partners from civic and community groups, government, and the private sector. This engagement took many forms, including one-on-one conversations, focus groups, advisory committees, and public events. Two advisory groups—the Steering Committee and Community Advisory Group—in particular provided essential guidance for the Assessment. WHO 700+ individuals from 450+ organizations engaged with MPC over the course of the Assessment. Participants came from: 80+ government agencies and departments, 200+ civic and community organizations, 24 ward offices, and 90+ private sector partners. 14 Steering Committee meetings + 7 Community Advisory Group meetings 21 advisory group meetings 50+ one-on-one conversations 10+ focus group sessions 5 public events and workshops For more detail on the ways that MPC engaged stakeholders and how stakeholder input informed this work, as well as a list of participating organizations in the Steering Committee and Community Advisory Group, see APPENDIX: ENGAGEMENT METHODOLOGY.

title: What is land use? What is zoning?
text: What is land use? What is zoning? Land use is how Chicagoans experience the places we live, work, and visit in our daily lives. The apartment building next door, the nearby park, that favorite corner store or local coffee shop, that empty lot or big-box store, the factory or car wash across the street—all are examples of different land uses. A zine to demystify zoning For more on zoning basics, a detailed history of zoning in Chicago, and the nitty-gritty of how zoning works, check out MPC’s zine, developed as part of the Assessment. MPC collaborated with the Assessment’s Community Advisory Group to develop In the Zone: A Chicagoan’s Guide to Zoning and Land Use . Available in physical and digital form—and in Spanish and Simplified Chinese—this illustrated resource is for anyone who wants to learn about zoning in Chicago. Zoning regulates land uses by setting limits on what can be built, and where. In this report, “zoning” includes the zoning ordinance (also known as the zoning code or text) which sets out rules for development in different zoning districts, the zoning map which determines the districts that apply to different areas of the city, and the zoning process—the people and pathways through which decisions about zoning get made. Together, these things determine which land uses are allowed in specific locations and set limits on new development’s size and shape. Zoning controls how tall a building can be and how close it can be to the street. It influences allowable density: how many of something, like homes or storefronts, exist in a space. Zoning also influences how long the development process takes, how much it costs, and who can weigh in along the way. Zoning reform isn’t a silver bullet. Many other factors also play an important role in shaping development and the feel of neighborhoods. This encompasses everything from other regulatory systems like building codes and business licensing, to the market for development (including what financing is available for development), taxes and other revenue structures, and community institutions that anchor neighborhoods. For more information on Chicago’s zoning districts, including each zoning designation’s share of city land—plus a map of zoning districts across the city—see APPENDIX: ZONING DISTRICTS . Why does zoning matter? Improving zoning means improving life for Chicagoans. Zoning is one of the most direct tools policymakers have to influence how neighborhoods look and feel. As the research in this report shows, our current zoning system does not always result in equitable outcomes. Zoning is part of a long, ongoing history of laws and practices that have contributed to a segregated Chicago, with disinvestment in some neighborhoods and abundant resources in others. Currently, zoning is controlled through a longstanding practice called “aldermanic prerogative.” Alderpersons have control over what gets built within the boundaries of each of our 50 wards. This approach has not been successful in meeting our challenges: Chicago is seen as too unpredictable a place to build, housing continues to become more expensive, and segregation continues to divide our city. We have an opportunity with zoning to think as a city, moving beyond a ward-by-ward system and taking a bigger-picture policy approach. For more on zoning basics and the history of zoning in Chicago, read MPC’s zine In the Zone: A Chicagoan’s Guide to Zoning and Land Use , developed as part of the Zoning Assessment.

title: how-conducted
text: How was the Assessment conducted? This section provides a high-level overview of the process of conducting the Assessment. For more detail, see APPENDIX: ENGAGEMENT METHODOLOGY and APPENDIX: RESEARCH METHODOLOGY . Defining core values and selecting outcomes to analyze To lay the groundwork for the project, MPC facilitated a series of monthly meetings with the project’s Steering Committee, composed of 42 members across a wide range of sectors, including city agency staff, environmental justice and housing advocates, community organizations, architects, planners, and real estate professionals. The Committee created shared definitions for core project values—equity, sustainability, and public health. Equity Outcomes and processes that result in fair and just access to opportunities and resources by way of repairing past harms and transforming power dynamics so that everyone, but particularly oppressed groups, both historically and presently, have the power and resources that they need to thrive. Sustainability An inclusive, systemic approach that improves and integrates environment, climate, health, social equity, and economic vitality in order to create thriving, healthy, diverse, and resilient communities and natural ecosystems for this generation and generations to come. Public health The physical, mental, and social wellbeing of individuals and neighborhoods and populations. All of these are shaped by social and physical structures, conditions, and processes. The Steering Committee also mapped out the zoning process and identified challenges based on their experiences. Finally, the Steering Committee developed a list of more than 120 outcomes of interest for the research. From that list, they selected 13 outcomes through consensus voting and discussion. Out of those 13 outcomes, based on the likelihood of a connection between the outcome and zoning, plus research feasibility, the research team selected seven priority outcomes for the research to focus on. The Steering Committee created shared definitions for these seven priority outcomes. more than 120 outcomes of interest 13 outcomes seven priority outcomes Affordable housing Diverse and affordable housing options (subsidized, affordable, workforce/middle, market, and luxury) are available in every neighborhood including for the job insecure and unhoused populations Strong business corridors Strong and vibrant business corridors with diverse business opportunities to support the economic needs and resiliency of every community Limited pollution exposure All neighborhoods feature low levels of pollution, taking into account cumulative impacts on overburdened communities Accessible public transit hubs All communities feature public transit options that are convenient and reliable, and serve hubs with housing, businesses, recreation and other services Available groceries and healthcare Affordable grocery options and healthcare providers are accessible in all neighborhoods Mitigation and adaptation to climate change All communities feature green infrastructure and energy-efficient building stock that both mitigates and adapts to climate change Productive land use All land in communities is used productively, meaning beneficial to local residents and aligned with community needs Conducting and refining the research For each of these seven priority outcomes, the research team approached the work in three stages. Understand the outcome: What is the current state of this outcome? How have trends shown up across neighborhoods in the city? How has this outcome changed over time? Understand the zoning: Which elements of zoning could be connected to this outcome? How are those elements distributed throughout the city? Understand the relationship: What can the data tell us about the connection between zoning and the outcome? To complete these analyses, the team first had to assemble foundational data on zoning and data related to each individual outcome. MPC compiled zoning data for three separate points in time: 2003, 2012, and 2023. 2 Having zoning data for three separate years allowed the team to track trends over time. Then, MPC compiled data on each individual outcome from a variety of sources. Analyses varied depending on available data—for example, some metrics could be longitudinally analyzed, while others could not. For each outcome, the research team refined the analysis through stakeholder engagement. Stakeholders provided feedback on initial drafts of the research during Steering Committee meetings, Community Advisory Group meetings, or public workshops, and the research team used that feedback to improve the analyses. MPC collected more than 1,200 pieces of written feedback while developing and refining the recommendations in this report. Developing the recommendations As with the research approach, stakeholders also informed the Assessment’s recommendations. In response to initial drafts of research results, stakeholders weighed in on which policy implications stood out to them, creating an initial list of possible policy directions. To further ground policy development, MPC also conducted a national scan of zoning best practices. MPC staff teams worked together to synthesize the research findings, policy implications from stakeholders, and best practices into preliminary policy recommendations. MPC teams then solicited feedback on these preliminary recommendations in a series of stakeholder workshops. Using dot boards, participants voted on the effectiveness of each recommendation, and provided written feedback on how the recommendations might impact their communities and how they might be strengthened. MPC collected more than 1,200 pieces of written feedback in response to the preliminary recommendations. MPC staff used this feedback to further refine the recommendations. As recommendations were finalized and themes emerged, the team moved from an outcome-based structure into the structure you see in this report, which aligns policy recommendations and research findings with five separate challenges and visions for zoning and land use.

title: The challenge: A worsening affordability crisis is pinching budgets and displacing Chicagoans
text: The challenge: A worsening affordability crisis is pinching budgets and displacing Chicagoans The challenge: A worsening affordability crisis is pinching budgets and displacing Chicagoans Terms you’ll see in this section affordable spending 30% or less of household income on housing costs by-right development development that falls within current zoning rules, without the need for rezoning or applying for zoning relief from the city downzoning changing an area’s zoning from a higher-density zoning district to a lower-density district Planned Development (PD) a zoning review process that involves directly negotiating elements of development with the city, and requires approval by City Council and the Chicago Plan Commission zoning envelope the total number of housing units the zoning code allows in a given area, sometimes referred to as “zoning capacity” As most households’ largest monthly expense, the cost of housing affects everyone. 3 MPC and the Urban Institute’s research found that the problem is worsening: housing has become significantly less affordable over the last 20 years, particularly for Black and Latinx residents. One key explanation is that we do not have enough housing in Chicago to meet demand, and we do not have enough affordable housing: the Chicago metro area is short 230,000 affordable rental homes for very low-income renter households. 4 But Chicago’s zoning code limits how much new housing can legally be built: it is illegal to build new multifamily housing on most of the city’s residential land without a zoning change, and most new multi-family housing gets built as Planned Developments—a process that adds time, money, and complication for developers. Our work also confirms what research 5 on downzoning and historic preservation in Chicago has shown—that these tools have functioned to create more exclusionary neighborhoods over time. Over the past two decades, housing has become increasingly unaffordable for all Chicagoans. By 2022, the typical Chicago household (a household with the median citywide income) could not afford to buy or rent the median home on much of the North and Northwest sides, because of these areas’ high housing prices. And across much of the South and West sides, households with typical income for a neighborhood would need to spend more than 30% of their income to rent the median home in that neighborhood. Chicago’s zoning code limits the amount of new housing that can be legally built in the city. Though half the city is zoned to allow homes, most of that land only allows very low density development. 53% of Chicago is set aside for homes through residential zoning. Most of that land (41% of the city) is zoned Residential Single-Family (RS), a zoning district that allows the construction of only single family homes, or two-flats in some limited circumstances. 6 This means 41% of the city is zoned to nearly always allow only the most expensive type of housing: detached single family homes. Note: Does not include parcels zoned for PD or PMD. Does not account for zoning bonuses. Created by Urban Institute. Source: Chicago zoning 2023 It is illegal to build new multi-family housing in much of the city without a zoning change. Just 11% of the city is zoned for multifamily housing development: 8% is zoned Residential Two-Flat, Townhouse, and Multi-Unit (RT), and 3% is zoned Residential Multi-Unit (RM). 7 This restrictive zoning policy leaves very little room to build new housing in large swaths of the city. This also means that across substantial portions of the city, much of the housing that already exists, such as two-to-four flats, would be illegal to build according to today’s rules. Significant portions of the city—the periphery of the city, as well as much of the Northwest side—have fully utilized the current zoning envelope, meaning current zoning cannot accommodate any more housing units in those areas. Other areas—the mid-South side and much of the near West side—do have room in the zoning envelope for housing development. Low-density residential zoning predominates even near transit. About half of Chicagoans live within a half-mile of a CTA ‘L’ station, and just 15% live within a quarter-mile, meaning they can get to a transit station by walking or using a mobility device in 5 minutes or less. One factor limiting the number of people who can live in transit-accessible housing is that a large amount of land near transit (26% of land within a half-mile of an ‘L’ station) is still zoned to allow only low-density residential development (RS), limiting access to both transit and housing. Citywide, a total of about 15 square miles of land is both within a half-mile radius of a CTA rail station and zoned RS. 60% of all new homes added in Chicago between 2006 and 2024 were in just 5 of Chicago’s 77 community areas: Near North Side, Near West Side, Loop, West Town, and Near South Side New housing is concentrated in just a few neighborhoods. Most community areas (45 out of 77) have built fewer than 500 new homes since 2006. The majority (60%) of the approximately 120,000 new housing units built in the city since 2006 were concentrated in just five community areas: Near North Side (19%); Near West Side (14%); Loop (13%); West Town (7%); Near South Side (7%). 8 Most new housing is being built through the Planned Development process. From 2006 to 2024, 58% of new housing units—and 68% of new housing units in projects with five or more units—were built as part of a Planned Development (PD), a type of zoning amendment and in-depth project review, as opposed to built under by-right zoning. This means Planned Developments are playing an outsized role in our development environment. For more on PDs, see page 17 . Permits for new housing, by project unit count, 2006-2024 New units permitted between 2006 and 2024. Most new multifamily units were constructed in Planned Development areas. Created by Urban Institute. Source: Building permit data, City of Chicago Designated affordable housing options are limited and distributed inequitably across Chicago. Some of the most common affordable housing units—federally subsidized units with guaranteed affordability for households with low and moderate incomes—are concentrated in a few communities on Chicago’s South and West sides and are sparse in the areas with predominantly white and high-income populations. Downzoning and historic preservation create more exclusionary neighborhoods. In the decades since 1970, City Council tended to downzone or designate for historic preservation areas with higher housing values and with predominantly white residents. 9 Compared to other neighborhoods, these areas had lower rates of housing construction, neighborhood demographics shifted to a higher share of white residents, and housing costs increased. This finding aligns with previous research about the impacts of downzoning and historic preservation in Chicago. 10 Deconversions of multifamily housing stock into single family homes results in housing supply losses that the city cannot afford. The DePaul Institute for Housing Studies found that between 2010 and 2023, the city lost nearly 23,000 units in two-to-four unit buildings, with the largest losses in lower-cost neighborhoods. 11 With so little of the city currently zoned to allow new two-to-four flats, the city has been unable to compensate for this housing loss.

title: The vision: Make space for more homes that Chicagoans can afford
text: The vision: Make space for more homes that Chicagoans can afford The vision: Make space for more homes that Chicagoans can afford Legalize 4-flats and ADUs citywide: At minimum, allow housing types with up to four units by-right and additional dwelling units (ADUs) in all residential areas. To create space for more housing, MPC recommends legalizing building types of up to at least four-flats on residential land across the city and updating accompanying bulk and density requirements to allow these types of construction. MPC also recommends legalizing additional dwelling units (ADUs) on all residential land. ADUs are additional homes connected to or outside an existing building (like a basement or attic apartment, or a coach house). Chicago’s City Council expanded ADU allowances in 2025, 12 but in the ongoing tradition of aldermanic prerogative, this expansion requires alders to opt-in any area zoned RS in their wards, rather than allowing ADUs by-right citywide. Allowing housing to be built more densely across the city would allow for more units that are typically more affordable than single family homes, while still fitting the current character of Chicago, where two-to-four flats and coach houses are common housing types. City Spotlights: Cities are making room for more housing Cities across the country are making changes to zoning to address the need for more homes. Some examples: Portland, OR (2020) passed zoning reforms allowing four-to-six unit buildings and ADUs in its lowest-density zoning districts. Cincinnati, OH (2024) passed a zoning reform called Connected Communities, allowing up to four-unit housing near transit. New York City, NY (2024) passed the City of Yes zoning reform plan, a change expected to enable the creation of 82,000 homes over 15 years. Madison, WI (2025) passed a proposal to allow two units of housing on any residential lot. Tulsa, OK (2024) made both citywide and neighborhood-specific changes to its zoning code to encourage more types of housing development. San Francisco, CA (2025) passed the Family Zoning Plan, which created capacity for more than 36,000 additional homes by increasing building height limits and allowing more homes to fit within existing height limits. The legislation also includes provisions for displaced legacy businesses, preservation protections for historic resources, and tenant protections. Legalize 6 stories near transit: At minimum, allow apartment buildings with up to 6 stories by-right near rail stations and the most frequent and highest-volume bus lines. There is room to allow more housing near transit, where residents have greater access to amenities and lower transportation costs. MPC recommends allowing six story multifamily buildings by-right in close proximity to transit, with an option to include commercial uses on the ground floor, and updating accompanying bulk and density requirements to allow these types of construction. Decrease reliance on Planned Developments for multifamily construction: Right-size thresholds for Planned Developments so more multifamily housing can be built by-right. The Planned Developments process was originally designed for larger, more complex developments like medical campuses, but the process is currently used for most new multi-family development in Chicago. In addition to other recommendations in this report that make it easier to build multi-family housing through the zoning code, increasing the thresholds that trigger the Planned Development process can help ensure Planned Development review is reserved for development types that require more review (such as certain manufacturing types, development on or near waterfronts, large institutions, or other sensitive development types). Apartment buildings, on the other hand, expand access to housing, do not reduce local home values, and fit into Chicago’s existing built form. As such, with minor exceptions, they should not undergo special review. For more on Planned Developments, see page 17 . Use zoning tools to promote deep affordability: Prioritize and incentivize affordable housing (fast-track zoning approvals for affordable development, prohibit reactive downzoning, and protect against the loss of naturally affordable units). Zoning changes that make room for more homes should be paired with policies that prioritize and incentivize the creation and preservation of homes affordable to the lowest-income Chicagoans. Even if we move towards affordability by addressing our supply challenges, market-rate housing will not meet the need for deeply affordable housing. Zoning changes that make room for more homes should be paired with policies that prioritize and incentivize the creation and preservation of homes affordable to the lowest-income Chicagoans. Though zoning cannot achieve this goal on its own, it is one part of a larger strategy. In addition to maintaining the city’s Affordable Requirements Ordinance, which requires certain multifamily development to include a set-aside number of affordable units, MPC recommends updating zoning policies to further support the creation of new income-limited affordable housing units. This could mean fast-tracking zoning approvals for affordable developments, and prohibiting downzoning in reaction to proposed affordable developments. Promoting affordability also means taking active steps to preserve existing affordable units. This requires funding to support acquisition and rehabilitation of properties. Without this funding, preservation strategies will be limited in their effectiveness. Nevertheless, zoning and land use policies can play a role: for example, expanding and strengthening the existing “Predominance of the Block” approach—which uses the housing already on a block to determine a context-appropriate density floor for development—could help protect against deconversion of multifamily housing, which tends to be more affordable, into single-family homes, which tend to be more expensive. This approach is currently only used in Chicago within designated geographic boundaries. Other protections could also be explored to specifically target local conditions in areas experiencing ongoing disinvestment or gentrification pressures.

title: Understanding Planned Developments
text: Understanding Planned Developments Some developments in Chicago go through a zoning process called the Planned Development process: a type of zoning amendment that must pass the Plan Commission and City Council for a development to move forward. This process was designed for large and complex projects, allowing developers and the City to directly negotiate and customize elements of development the zoning code usually regulates directly, via a unique agreement that covers multiple buildings across a site. This includes land uses, bulk and density, and open space or other public amenities that are included as part of a development. The PD process also mandates that the developer hold at least one public meeting on the project. The PD process is a required step for some unusual types of developments on lots above a certain size, like hospitals, airports, universities, and sports arenas. Depending on the zoning district, the process can also be required for buildings that are taller than a designated height, or include more than a designated number of housing units, among other situations. 13 Some developments have the choice of going through the PD process, or opting out. Planned Developments are now the main pathway for housing development in Chicago: 58% of all new homes added in Chicago between 2006 and 2024 were added through the PD process PDs have become the most common zoning pathway for housing development in Chicago. From 2003 to 2023, Chicago created more than 600 PDs, together replacing by-right zoning with the Planned Development designation on an additional 5.8 square miles of land. By 2023, there were a total of about 1,400 PDs in Chicago. These PDs cover about 13% of zoned land. In recent years, PDs have been the main pathway for adding new housing units in the city. Urban Institute found that 58% of all new homes added in Chicago between 2006 and 2024 were added through the PD process, meaning each project was individually reviewed by the Plan Commission and City Council. In addition, most dense residential development happened through the PD process: among new housing units added in projects with five or more units, 68% were part of a PD. Smaller PDs are increasingly common. Most of the new PDs added over the last 20 years (about two-thirds) are relatively small in terms of their land area, covering less than 150,000 square feet. In 2003, there were more medium- and large-sized PDs (above 150,000 square feet) than smaller ones; by 2023, it was more common to see smaller PDs. Currently, information about PDs is only accessible by reviewing individual Planned Development Agreements, rather than a central dataset. For this reason, PDs were a gap in our research for the Zoning Assessment: our calculation of the total residentially-zoned land in the city, for example, does not include PDs, since each PD varies in use type, and that information is not centralized by the City. MPC is currently building a dataset to better understand PDs, and we anticipate sharing findings from this dataset in the future.

title: The challenge: Jobs and business vitality are inequitably distributed
text: The challenge: Jobs and business vitality are inequitably distributed The challenge: Jobs and business vitality are inequitably distributed Strong transit-connected business corridors provide employment and wealth-building opportunities, neighborhood amenities, and walkable shared space. But MPC research shows that business and commercial activity—measured through business concentration and vacancy rates—is inequitably distributed across Chicago. Although zoning is not necessarily the exclusive cause of these outcomes, our analysis identified inequities in the distribution of pedestrian-oriented zoning designations and zoning for car-dominated businesses—highlighting the opportunity to take a citywide approach to encouraging walkable, vibrant pedestrian-oriented business corridors. These corridors can be cornerstones of economic growth, tools to reduce vacancies, and landing places for small businesses. Businesses are more highly concentrated in census tracts with higher shares of white population and lower shares of Black population. In majority-white census tracts, there were an average of 14.7 businesses per 1,000 residents in 2023, compared with 8.6 businesses per 1,000 residents in majority-Black census tracts. Combined business and residential property vacancy rates show similar disparities across racial and ethnic groups , with majority-Black tracts possessing vacancy rates (10%) over three times greater than majority-white (3%) and five times greater than majority-Asian census tracts (2%) in 2022. Identifies addresses that have not collected mail for 90 days or longer; includes both residential and business locations. City Spotlight: Mixed-use zoning When Columbus, OH began updating its 70-year-old zoning code, it was clear that building more housing alone wouldn’t create vibrant communities. Columbus’s “Zone In” plan, adopted by its City Council in 2024, approached development holistically, establishing mixed-use districts citywide. 140 miles of key corridors across the whole city will allow 88,000 more units of housing alongside more spaces for businesses and essential services. With different zoning allowances across six types of mixed-use districts, Columbus created more flexibility to build complete communities: more homes supporting affordability, more customers for local businesses, more jobs and lively streets, anchored around transit that allows people to save time and money when moving around the city. Black and Latinx Chicagoans are more likely than white and Asian Chicagoans to live near zoning for auto-oriented business (B3 and C zoning), as opposed to other business districts that encourage retail for pedestrians. Citywide trends show correlations between greater shares of the more automobile-oriented zoning districts (B3 and C) and more businesses, jobs, and consumer spending. However, B1 and B2 zoning, which are not oriented toward car traffic, can help contribute to business corridor vibrancy. Zoning for “pedestrian streets,” areas designed as walkable business corridors, is concentrated on the North side. Pedestrian streets are streets designated in the zoning code that must follow certain pedestrian-friendly street design standards. Making a street an official pedestrian street currently requires a zoning change, in which individual alders opt in a specific street in their ward. Importantly, only some business corridors—those with high concentrations of stores and restaurants, and with low vacancy—are currently eligible for the designation. Pedestrian streets are concentrated on the North side. Of Chicago’s 62 pedestrian streets outside of downtown, only 12 are not on the North side. Zoning districts that allow businesses and mixed-uses—B, C, and D districts—tend to concentrate near transit. However, a significant amount of low-density residential zoning still exists near transit. Of the total land in the city that is zoned to allow businesses and mixed-use development (B, C, and D districts), 41% is within a half-mile of a CTA rail station. By comparison, 25% of all zoned land in the city is within a half-mile of a CTA rail station. However, a large share of the total land near transit stations (26%) is still zoned to only allow low-density residential development (RS), limiting the potential for transit-connected businesses and more housing. Citywide, a total of about 15 square miles of land is both within a half-mile radius of a CTA rail station and zoned RS. title: The vision: Clear the way for vibrant, livable communities
text: The vision: Clear the way for vibrant, livable communities The vision: Clear the way for vibrant, livable communities Zone for a dynamic mix of uses near transit: Allow more opportunities for Chicagoans to live, work, and visit places near transit, especially in areas with fewer jobs and/or higher vacancy rates. In addition to allowing more housing near transit (see page 16 ), MPC recommends adjusting zoning near transit to support the development of mixed-use employment hubs and business corridors, especially in areas with fewer jobs and higher vacancy rates where minimizing barriers to development is one step towards revitalization. This may require reevaluating business and commercial zoning district categories to ensure that districts are flexible enough, allowing both residential uses and a wide enough range of commercial uses. Expand pedestrian streets near transit: Standardize the use of the pedestrian street designation near transit and modernize pedestrian street eligibility and standards. Currently the “pedestrian street” designation is a limited, preservation-oriented tool, allowing individual alders to opt-in to pedestrian friendliness standards for specific, eligible streets. This treats pedestrian friendliness as an exceptional case requiring additional legislation and approvals, while streetscapes that are hostile to pedestrians are considered the status quo. Our current approach has had inequitable outcomes, with pedestrian streets concentrated on the North side. MPC recommends standardizing the proactive use of the pedestrian street designation on business corridors near transit citywide, while making allowances for preexisting uses and exceptional situations, like transit along highways. MPC also recommends strengthening the definition of the pedestrian street designation itself. This means including a list of prohibited and explicitly allowed uses in the definition, limiting future downzonings, and updating eligibility criteria to allow pedestrian streets to be used as a forward-looking planning tool citywide. A standardized, expanded set of pedestrian streets could also be anchors for citywide planning efforts discussed on page 31 . Bring small-scale business into neighborhoods: Increase the types of businesses allowed in residential neighborhoods. Currently, only a very limited number of businesses—such as bed and breakfasts and vacation rentals—are allowed in residential districts (and even then, only in some districts). “Business Live/Work Units” and “Artist Live/Work Units” are only allowed in areas zoned for business and commercial use, often also requiring approval by the Zoning Board of Appeals. Allowing small-scale, low-impact businesses like corner stores, cafes, small-scale retail, and artist studios is a step toward improving the livability of neighborhoods and supporting small business development.

title: The challenge: Too many Chicagoans are exposed to unhealthy pollutants and vulnerable to climate impacts
text: The challenge: Too many Chicagoans are exposed to unhealthy pollutants and vulnerable to climate impacts The challenge: Too many Chicagoans are exposed to unhealthy pollutants and vulnerable to climate impacts Terms you’ll see in this section pollution waste that contaminates our air, land, and water; in this analysis, measured through an index that includes many different types of pollution, released by U.S. EPA air pollution small particulates in the air, also known as PM2.5, known to have harmful effects on health; in this analysis, estimated using satellite data, from researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago combined heat + flood susceptibility an index combining multiple data sources on flooding and felt heat (accounting for both all-day temperature and humidity), compiled by MPC Environmental hazards like pollution, heat, and flooding are major threats to Chicagoans’ health and well-being. 14 Our analysis shows that all Chicagoans are being exposed to air pollution at unhealthy levels, but some populations, particularly Latinx Chicagoans, are much more exposed than others. Susceptibility to heat and flooding are likewise inequitably distributed, with Black and Latinx Chicagoans overrepresented in the areas more likely to experience climate impacts. The majority of land in Chicago with high heat and flood susceptibility is zoned for residential use, meaning adapting residential land to also address climate change through both mitigation and adaptation will be essential to combat these climate risks. The research also shows a strong correlation between manufacturing zoning and pollution levels. Black and Latinx Chicagoans tend to see larger amounts of land zoned for manufacturing, and a greater likelihood of heavier manufacturing in their neighborhoods. All Chicagoans breathe unhealthy air. All across the city, Chicagoans are exposed to small particulate air pollution at higher levels than recommended by 2024 US EPA public health standards for long-term exposure (9 micrograms per cubic meter). Estimated levels across Chicago range from about 9 to 12 micrograms per cubic meter on an average summer day. Latinx Chicagoans experience the most pollution exposure—and the least tree coverage, which can be a protective factor against pollution, as well as heat and flood risks. Though Latinx populations make up 30% of the citywide population, they comprise 50% of the population in the highest (top fifth) air pollution census tracts and 37% of the population in the highest (top fifth) overall pollution tracts. The parts of the city with higher pollution levels—near downtown, along expressways, and along major industrial corridors—also tend to have low levels of tree coverage. In the areas of the city with the most tree coverage (canopy coverage of 25% or more), only 16% of the population is Latinx. Areas with manufacturing zoning tend to have higher levels of pollution. A substantial portion of the city—17% of zoned land—is zoned for manufacturing (M or PMD zoning). Manufacturing zoning and pollution levels are correlated: a greater share of manufacturing zoning within a neighborhood tends to correspond to greater exposure to pollution in that neighborhood. Census tracts that contain manufacturing zoning have a higher pollution index, on average, and pollution levels tend to increase as the share of the tract zoned for manufacturing increases. For example, in the top 30% of tracts with the most Latinx Chicagoans, 29% of the land is zoned for manufacturing. Interactive chart redrawn for this site from the figures printed in the source. Latinx and Black Chicagoans tend to have more land in their neighborhoods zoned for heavy manufacturing, and manufacturing overall, compared to other groups. 23% of land is zoned for manufacturing in areas most populated by Black Chicagoans, while 29% of land is zoned for manufacturing in areas most populated by Latinx Chicagoans. 15 This compares to only 6% and 9% of land zoned this way in areas most populated by white and Asian Chicagoans, respectively. In areas where most Black and Latinx Chicagoans live, manufacturing zoning is also much more likely to be for heavy industry (M3 zoning). Different neighborhoods face different types and levels of climate challenges, which require different solutions. Some neighborhoods face urban heat challenges, others experience urban flooding challenges, and some face both. Multipronged mitigation and adaptation strategies are required to adequately address climate challenges. Neighborhoods also have different types and availabilities of land for implementing mitigation and adaptation strategies, such as vacant land, City-owned properties, and land uses with a large amount of pavement (like industrial land and heavy arterials). All-day heat index Flooding index Combined heat and flooding index Source: City of Chicago 2023 Cool Chi/Heat Watch, Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning (CMAP), City of Chicago data portal Black and Latinx residents are overrepresented in the areas more likely to see climate impacts. In the top fifth of tracts for heat and flood susceptibility, Black and Latinx Chicagoans comprise 83% of the population, despite comprising 57% of the city’s total population. Meanwhile, white Chicagoans are underrepresented in those same tracts. While white residents make up 33% of the city’s total population, they make up only 14% of the population in the top fifth highest heat and flood susceptibility tracts. Racial and ethnic composition by combined heat + flood index Source: Census ACS 2018-2022 Interactive chart redrawn for this site from the figures printed in the source. The majority of land in tracts with high heat and flood susceptibility are zoned for single family homes. More than 60% of land in the top fifth most heat and flood susceptible tracts is zoned RS (Residential Single-Unit), which is the lowest-density residential zoning district. The disparate susceptibility in low-density districts could have implications for long-term affordability for individual homeowners as costs rise in these areas, but further exploration of the impacts is needed to understand this finding and what it means both for affordability and for adaptation and mitigation strategies. On the flip side, areas zoned Parks and Open Space, particularly along Lake Michigan, are least susceptible. Certain land use factors can be protective against climate challenges, and others can worsen susceptibility—but climate patterns are complex, not straightforward. In general, tree canopy, green stormwater infrastructure, and energy-efficient buildings function as protective factors against heat and flooding susceptibility. Impervious surfaces, older housing stock, and heavy traffic patterns can worsen susceptibility to climate challenges. These factors are not determinant—they don’t automatically translate to risk levels at a citywide level—but we can see impacts at a neighborhood level, particularly looking at tree coverage as a cooling factor that helps with heat events. Chicago’s fractured tree governance Trees are powerful infrastructure, providing a host of benefits to neighborhoods: cleaner air, shade and cooling, greener streets, and protection against growing climate risks. But addressing gaps in tree coverage is an ongoing challenge. One element of this challenge: Chicago has a complex and fractured system of tree governance. Many of Chicago’s trees sit in the parkway, the area between the sidewalk and the street. City law says that the City owns these trees. However, a part of the zoning code called the Landscape Ordinance requires that developers undertaking certain types of new construction or rehabilitation projects plant trees in the parkway. In those cases—usually residential development of more than three units or parking lots above a certain size—developers must get approval for their planting plans from the Department of Planning and Development. To do the planting, developers must hire a contractor specifically licensed to work in the public way. Developers need clearance from the Department of Transportation to excavate, and a permit from Department of Streets and Sanitation’s Bureau of Forestry, which regulates trees in the parkway. After planting, the Landscape Ordinance gives the responsibility for routine maintenance of these required trees to property owners—except for tree trimming, removal, and other work affecting a tree’s health or structure, which is handled by the Bureau of Forestry. To further complicate the picture, plenty of trees are outside the parkway. Chicago Park District stewards trees on park land. Chicago Public Schools controls trees on school property. And trees on street medians, usually arterial streets medians or roundabouts, are the responsibility of the Chicago Department of Transportation (CDOT) or in some cases, the Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT). For example, PM2.5 air pollution causes an estimated 5% of all premature deaths in the city. title: The vision: Integrate healthy air, water, and land into zoning and land use practices
text: The vision: Integrate healthy air, water, and land into zoning and land use practices The vision: Integrate healthy air, water, and land into zoning and land use practices Update zoning for modern industry: Re-classify manufacturing and industrial uses based on measurable benefits and harms—such as jobs, pollution, environmental impacts, and public health impacts—to encourage low-impact, job-dense industry. The zoning code currently classifies manufacturing and industrial uses into four categories (Artisan, Limited, General, and Intensive). These categories are based on use, rather than impact. The zoning code currently does not attempt to estimate the benefits and burdens of a proposed industrial development, which may be a complex mix of positive and negative impacts for workers, residents, and the city—factors such as jobs, pollution, environmental impact, and public health. MPC recommends modernizing the zoning code to holistically account for the ways industrial land uses impact their surrounding communities. This could include air pollution, noise pollution, truck and transportation impacts, wages, and job creation. In addition, MPC recommends separating heavier industrial uses from residential areas and maintaining minimum distances between these uses, as well as other protective strategies like stronger requirements for vegetative buffers around industrial uses, which can help mitigate pollution exposure. Protect overburdened communities from cumulative impacts: Require a holistic review of the expected health and quality-of-life impacts of all proposed intensive industrial facilities. The Chicago Department of Public Health has developed a cumulative impacts assessment that measures how multiple environmental burdens and social stressors combine to affect health across neighborhoods. MPC recommends using this tool to evaluate future heavy industrial developments, particularly to ensure that highly intensive industrial facilities do not cause additional harms to overburdened communities. Additional layers of zoning review for heavy industrial facilities—through special use approval or the Planned Development process—can provide the opportunity to conduct this evaluation. City Spotlight: Washington DC Washington, D.C.’s Green Area Ratio (GAR) is a zoning regulation implemented in 2013 to reduce stormwater runoff, improve air quality, and mitigate urban heat. Based on a property’s zoning district, the GAR sets a minimum score that new construction or major renovation projects must meet. Starting with a minimum lot area requirement for landscaping or sustainable site design, the GAR assigns multipliers to different strategies, like tree planting, permeable pavements, or renewable energy systems, based on their impact. Project teams must show that their site design will fulfill a property’s required GAR performance score as part of their building permit application. Since the program’s inception, over 184 hectares of green infrastructure have been built, which is nearly one-and-a-half times the size of Grant Park. Leverage unbuilt land for permeable surfaces: Use zoning to ensure unbuilt land helps counter flood and heat risk by requiring or incentivizing permeable surfaces and green infrastructure in setbacks, open space, parkways, and parking lots. The zoning code requires properties in some zoning districts, primarily residential, to retain unbuilt space as “setbacks” or “open space.” These are areas like front yards, back yards, and side walkways. The current ordinance does not require that these spaces include permeable surfaces or green infrastructure. Incorporating these as requirements or incentives could help reduce the impacts of heat and flooding. The code also regulates landscaping in and around parking lots and parkways, which are the space between the sidewalk and the street. Parking lots smaller than 1,200 square feet do not require screening from the street, and lots smaller than 3,000 square feet do not require internal planting. Parkway trees are not currently required for the development of single-family homes (our most common zoning district), two-flats, or three-flats. MPC recommends strengthening the requirements for permeable surfaces and planting in these spaces to increase the city’s resilience to heat and flooding challenges. Target climate-vulnerable areas for mitigation strategies: Prioritize communities most vulnerable to heat and flooding for more green space and remediation. Heat, flooding, and pollution exposure are not equally distributed across the city. As MPC’s research in the section above shows, Black and Latinx communities are most likely to face climate impacts. As part of a comprehensive planning process, areas disproportionately affected by climate impacts should be prioritized for investment in climate mitigation and adaptation strategies, such as converting city-owned vacant land to green space, targeted remediation funding, and green infrastructure projects.

title: The challenge: Zoning and land use policy is opaque and difficult to navigate
text: The challenge: Zoning and land use policy is opaque and difficult to navigate The challenge: Zoning and land use policy is opaque and difficult to navigate At least 28 geographic overlays exist in the zoning code, layered on top of standard zoning districts. Navigating zoning in Chicago can be extremely complex. There are at least 67 zoning districts, 16 with at least 28 geographic overlays layered on top of these districts. 17 At least 180 specific land use types are listed in the zoning code, and at least five government decision-making bodies 18 make official decisions about zoning. Contingencies and overlay geographies written into the code can make identifying specific requirements, like setbacks and other bulk and density requirements, a mazelike task. Adding to all this complexity is the reality of aldermanic control over zoning decisions, which takes a variety of forms across wards, as well as the increasingly common use of Planned Developments as a development vehicle (see page 17 ). For a resident interested in understanding how zoning impacts their neighborhood, excess complexity can make city government inaccessible, which erodes trust. And when complexity becomes standard, even for types of development that meet citywide goals, the result is added costs and delays, creating an unpredictable development environment. Those with the resources to navigate the system and weather delays—such as land use attorneys and/or surplus financing—are the ones who benefit. One place this dynamic plays out is the zoning landscape for small businesses. To better understand how zoning complexity impacts small businesses, MPC examined processes like the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) 19 , a quasi-judicial voting body that the city must have for property owners to appeal zoning decisions. The ZBA reviews requests for certain types of “zoning relief,” specific exemptions from zoning rules: special uses, which are land uses allowed with additional review in specific districts; variations, which are designated changes to bulk and density requirements; and appeals of zoning decisions made by the Zoning Administrator at the Department of Planning and Development. MPC’s research found that: 11 out of 12 applications that are reviewed by the Zoning Board of Appeals are approved The Zoning Board of Appeals approves most applications it receives. The ZBA approves 92% of applications and explicitly denies only about 3% to 4%, with the remainder being withdrawn from consideration by the applicant. ZBA members rarely disagree, with members voting unanimously in 96% of the votes the board takes. The majority of applications are variations (56%) or special uses (43%) and a very small number (less than 1%) are appeals. Although officially, alders are not part of the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) decision-making process, in practice, they hold major sway. These applications often require political support to move forward. The special use process is a barrier for small businesses. Most special use applications (78%) come from business-oriented (B and C) zoning districts. These are applications for a range of uses, including beauty salons, tattoo shops, outdoor patios, and community centers. Guided by recommendations provided by the Department of Planning and Development, the ZBA reviews an average of approximately 230 special use applications every year. Despite improvements to the application in recent years, navigating the ZBA is a complex, lengthy process, often requiring the help of an attorney. The opacity of the process and lack of consistent guidelines for the ZBA end up favoring applicants with time and resources to navigate the process, creating a pay-to-play system. And although officially, alders are not part of the ZBA decision-making process, in practice, alders hold major sway in the outcome of a ZBA application, so these applications often require political support to move forward. Additional costs and delays can stall or shutter a small business that’s otherwise ready to open. The outcome is a system that favors applicants with greater access to resources. Beauty and nail salons and barber shops are particularly affected by the ZBA. 27% of special use applications are for hair, nail, or beauty salons or barber shops, which are approved by the ZBA (95%) and decided in their first hearing (90%) at even higher rates than special uses overall. These businesses are permitted by-right in B districts—but only if they are not within 1,000 feet of another hair salon, in which case they need special use approval from the ZBA. This is a requirement that likely disproportionately affects woman-owned and immigrant-owned small businesses. 20 Variations are impacting residential development, particularly in areas zoned for more density. Most variation applications (68%) during the time period in our dataset came from residential districts. Variations also disproportionately originated in higher-density residential districts (RT and RM). While only 11% of residential land in the city is zoned RT or RM, 61% of variations from residential districts came from RT or RM districts. Additional research is needed to better understand these trends and how variations may be impacting housing development. 27% of special uses applications are for hair, nail, or beauty salons or barber shops, 95% of which are approved by the ZBA Data about zoning decisions is not generally released to the public in a standardized, searchable format. In the case of ZBA meetings and Planned Development agreements, information is released in the form of individual meeting-by-meeting or project-by-project PDFs. In both of these cases, in order to better understand these processes, MPC needed to compile unique datasets manually by pulling information from hundreds of PDFs. No publicly searchable dataset exists, which could be helpful for a potential small business owner to find examples of previous special use applications. In the case of administrative adjustments, no information is released publicly at all. Meanwhile, zoning amendments occur in the form of individual ordinances passed through City Council. These are accessible to those who know how to navigate the City Clerk’s website, but there is no public dataset that would allow for a systematic review of zoning amendment applications, which could have important implications for zoning policy. title: The vision: Clarify and streamline zoning process and categories
text: The vision: Clarify and streamline zoning process and categories The vision: Clarify and streamline zoning process and categories Modernize special uses: Permit most current special use categories by-right, with accompanying use standards. Require ZBA review only for uses with likely impacts on health and safety. For uses with likely impacts on health and safety—uses like heavy manufacturing, waste processing facilities, and adult-oriented uses, among others—the additional layer of review and transparency that the ZBA provides is warranted. But for the majority of uses that currently go through the special use process—including but not limited to uses like salons, live-work spaces, and community centers—this zoning review is serving as a barrier for small businesses. Instead of imposing exceptional review for these uses, MPC recommends that they be regulated like all other business types, and permitted by-right in the zoning districts where they are currently only possible as a special use. When businesses are subject to ZBA approval, the process should be simple enough to navigate without the need for a lawyer. MPC recommends removing the requirement that single-room occupancy buildings, shelters, and other group living quarters seeking to open in many zoning districts obtain special use approval. This requirement delays or blocks a necessary housing option that offers health and safety for our lowest-resourced neighbors. Reassess other zoning relief categories: Conduct a review of variation and administrative adjustment requests to determine zoning code updates. Broadly, variations and administrative adjustments (another type of zoning relief approved by the Zoning Administrator at DPD) tend to be requests for exceptions to bulk and density limits, such as setbacks or open space requirements. A thorough review is needed to understand the complexities of variations and administrative adjustments, particularly their impact on housing development. When these changes become commonplace, it’s often a signal that the zoning code and map need to be updated, and these relief mechanisms have become pay-to-play loopholes. A review is needed to better understand the nuances of specific types of variations and administrative adjustments, including whether zoning relief also plays a role in facilitating the deconversion of multifamily housing into single-family homes, decreasing housing supply. One clear opportunity for improvement is the variation for businesses seeking public place of amusement licenses near low-density residential districts. This is an outlier among variations, as it is a use type, rather than a bulk and density requirement. Bizarrely, applicants who are seeking a business license must legally argue they are not applying for the variation “based exclusively upon a desire to make more money out of the property”—a requirement that unnecessarily limits potential small businesses seeking to establish “third spaces” in neighborhoods. Centralize information about zoning: Provide a central hub for plain-language materials around zoning standards and processes, prioritizing information that facilitates housing and small business development. Zoning gets very technical, very fast. The Department of Planning and Development has been making significant strides in making zoning accessible, as demonstrated by their production of the Zoning Design Guidebook , which provides information on zoning regulations for property owners and developers in multiple languages. 21 The City can build on this milestone by centralizing this and other resources about zoning and development—such as a more user-friendly zoning map, resources on business zoning and business licensing, and information on financial supports for development—in a single online hub, and optimizing this hub for web searches. Where it is not possible to explain zoning rules in plain language, MPC recommends that the standard or process be re-evaluated, as excessive complexity can be a barrier to entry for newer and smaller-scale developers. Close zoning data gaps: Standardize and publicize data on zoning processes and outcomes. The lack of standardized data on zoning processes, including Zoning Board of Appeals applications, Planned Development agreements, and zoning amendments, is holding Chicago back. Up-to-date, standardized, and searchable datasets would build trust in government by increasing transparency into opaque processes, while advancing research that can improve zoning policy.
