title: The challenge: Proactive planning is piecemeal and focused on the neighborhood level
text: The challenge: Proactive planning is piecemeal and focused on the neighborhood level The challenge: Proactive planning is piecemeal and focused on the neighborhood level In Chicago, our efforts to update zoning tend to be piecemeal—and always at the discretion of the local alder—rather than guided by citywide planning and citywide goals. Chicago does not regularly engage in comprehensive citywide planning. The We Will Chicago Plan , adopted by the Chicago Plan Commission in 2023, was Chicago’s first citywide plan in more than 50 years. Chicago doesn’t lack ambitious aspirations for its future: We Will Chicago set out more than 40 goals and 150 objectives for the next ten years. But the Plan was not designed as a “comprehensive” plan, meaning it does not offer specific land use reforms to help translate its goals into reality or carry any statutory requirements for implementation. There is also no requirement for regular updates or review of the We Will Chicago Plan, which was tied to a mayoral administration, rather than an ongoing city strategy. Chicago’s last comprehensive planning effort dates back to 1966. 22 There is currently no mandate to comprehensively plan or regularly update zoning and land use policies as the city’s needs change. Instead, zoning changes often happen in response to specific development proposals—through rezonings for individual projects or through the Planned Development process—and through localized corridor planning initiatives. Currently, these changes require passage through City Council, which virtually always means deferring to the local alderperson. Without citywide planning directives to steer development decisions, each ward fends for itself. Public input may occur during public meetings of decision-making bodies, community meetings, and ward-level zoning advisory councils, but this is contingent on project specifics and on each alder’s interest in—and approach to—public engagement. Without a comprehensive planning process and a citywide approach, it is difficult if not impossible to make the changes we need at scale. Local corridor planning is valuable, but limited in its reach. Between 2024 and 2026, DPD has worked with local alders on corridor-by-corridor zoning changes, leading 16 rezoning efforts across 17 wards and encompassing at least 5,300 parcels. These initiatives are meaningful and show the benefits of moving beyond a parcel-by-parcel approach to zoning. Still, corridor planning is valuable but not sufficient: MPC estimates these rezonings cover less than 1% of total parcels in the city. Without a comprehensive planning process and a citywide approach, it is difficult if not impossible to make the changes we need at scale. Currently, zoning decisions ostensibly allow for public input, but a multiplicity of meetings and lack of clarity makes for a complex and inaccessible system. 23 Because these meetings are subject to the Illinois Open Meetings Act, they are open to the public and must include an opportunity for public comment. But that’s just about where the similarities end: whether public feedback actually matters for the decision itself, how the meetings are scheduled and publicized, and how public comment works varies widely. Plus, other meetings that also have an influence on zoning decisions, like ward-level zoning advisory councils, may or may not be subject to the Open Meetings Act. Without intentional and broad-reaching effort, public input often fails to be representative. There are persistent problems with public feedback that need to be proactively addressed. A public meeting on an individual rezoning, for example, tends to leave out some important groups: those who would like to weigh in but don’t have the resources; the unknown number of people who may feel small-scale harm or benefit, which can collectively add up to a large impact; and any future residents of any development enabled by the rezoning, who don’t live there yet. Research on public engagement patterns in Louisville showed that public speakers in rezoning hearings are more likely to be residents from whiter and higher-income neighborhoods. 24 This tracks with other research showing that opposition to development is more likely to come from older, white homeowners than others who live in a community. 25 Engagement that is larger than a single-project scope can begin to address some of these shortcomings, bringing in some of the voices that are missing when the conversation is limited to a single development. title: The vision: Tie zoning to foundational citywide planning and engagement
text: The vision: Tie zoning to foundational citywide planning and engagement The vision: Tie zoning to foundational citywide planning and engagement Periodically update zoning to align with a planning vision: Require regular reviews of the zoning code and map based on comprehensive citywide planning that meaningfully engages the public. MPC recommends that Chicago regularly engage in comprehensive citywide planning and meaningfully engage the public in coordinated neighborhood planning that connects to a citywide comprehensive plan. Comprehensive planning could reconcile competing priorities; guide the development of vibrant, walkable business corridors across the city; buffer high-impact industry from homes; address our climate-related vulnerabilities; and make room for the homes that we need as a city to address our affordability crisis. Comprehensive planning can also be a tool to guide public investment. It is essential that this comprehensive citywide planning be durable and long-term enough to extend beyond individual mayoral administrations; tied to mandated corresponding land use updates; and reliably budgeted and staffed by the City. Improve public input processes: Create a more standardized, transparent, and equitable public input process for public input on land use. MPC envisions shifting away from the status quo of projct-by-project community meetings as projects wind their way through various decision-making bodies. Instead, we recommend that public feedback occur at the neighborhood and city level, feeding into coordinated neighborhood and city planning. With this shift, there also needs to be an updated approach to public engagement itself. Where there are opportunities for public input on neighborhood and city planning, this engagement should be conducted in standardized and predictable ways across neighborhoods or wards, guided by a central coordinating agency. Within the bounds of predetermined policy must-haves, such as the need for more affordable housing, participants should be able to meaningfully change the outcome, and that process should be genuinely accessible to all who are interested in participating. This could mean, as a starting point, approaches such as: clear messaging in advance about what is being decided, how the public can weigh in, and what can or cannot legally be considered in that decision holding meetings in neighborhoods, rather than City Hall, and at a time outside of traditional business hours intentionally recruiting participants through local organizations and institutions reducing barriers with support for transportation, childcare, translation, or compensation. 26 City Spotlight: Minneapolis, Minnesota COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING Minnesota state statute requires local governments in the Twin Cities metropolitan area to keep their comprehensive plans up to date and consistent with zoning rules and regional planning goals. Local governments must review their comprehensive plans at least every 10 years. The local governments must update their plans as needed to stay consistent with the regional planning organization’s plan. Zoning and other local regulations must generally match the comprehensive plan. When plans are updated, neighboring communities and affected public agencies get an opportunity to review and comment. In 2019, Minneapolis’ 2040 Comprehensive Plan included recommendations for major land use reforms, like the legalization of duplexes and triplexes citywide, and increased density allowance along transit and commercial corridors. This comprehensive planning process led to concrete changes to the zoning code. PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT In 2007, the Minneapolis City Council adopted the Core Principles of Community Engagement from The International Association of Public Participation. These principles were expanded in the “Blueprint for Equitable Engagement” in 2015. The City of Minneapolis’ Neighborhood and Community Relations Department follows this blueprint department-wide, and it was used to facilitate meaningful public engagement in the 2040 Comprehensive Plan. For more on best practices for equitable public engagement, see “Exploring zoning-related public engagement | Part 2/2” on MPC’s website. ↩

title: Conclusion
text: Conclusion Chicago’s current zoning and land use system is not working at the scale or speed our challenges require, nor is it producing equitable outcomes. Much of this report is technical by necessity. It recommends changes to: what can be built by-right; when discretionary review should be required; how uses are classified; and how zoning decisions are made. But those changes add up to a larger civic choice: whether Chicago will continue to manage change parcel-by-parcel and ward-by-ward, or build a more equitable land-use system capable of responding to citywide needs. Making that shift will require addressing aldermanic prerogative and the ward-by-ward decision-making it reinforces. Too many land use decisions are still made reactively through individual exceptions and local negotiations. That leaves Chicago poorly equipped to address challenges that cross neighborhood and ward boundaries. Housing affordability, economic opportunity, environmental health, and climate resilience are citywide concerns; the policies that shape them should operate at a citywide scale. A more intentional approach would put a citywide framework in place before a specific development is on the table. Chicago could establish clearer citywide expectations, reserve discretionary review for projects that genuinely require it, and give residents a meaningful role in shaping the plans and standards that guide change. Neighborhoods have different histories and needs, and citywide policy should respond to those differences. But local variation should exist within a framework that also reflects Chicago’s shared responsibilities. Chicago’s racial and economic segregation did not develop separately from decisions about land use, housing, and investment. Those choices have distributed opportunity and burden unevenly across race and class, with effects that intersect with gender inequality and other forms of disadvantage. Zoning reform cannot undo that history, but it can change rules and processes that continue to reinforce those patterns. A more equitable land use system should help break down barriers between people and opportunity, rather than reproduce them for another generation. A more equitable land use system should help break down barriers between people and opportunity, rather than reproduce them for another generation. The recommendations in this Assessment offer practical steps that Chicago can take now, while pointing toward a broader shift in how the city plans for growth and change. But this work also has significance beyond Chicago. The specific solutions will differ from city to city, but the Assessment offers a model for approaching reform: define the outcomes a city wants, examine how existing land-use policies shape them, combine quantitative research with community and stakeholder experience, and translate that evidence into locally grounded policy. Chicago has an opportunity to demonstrate how cities can develop ambitious land use reform through a rigorous and inclusive process, building the capacity to make durable choices at a city scale. We can connect reform with repair, plan more deliberately for Chicago’s future, and lead with a model for other cities navigating the same challenges.

title: Appendix: Additional research findings
text: Appendix: Additional research findings This section contains key research findings for two outcome analyses that were not included in the body of this report: productive land use, and available groceries and healthcare. To view comprehensive research findings for these and other outcome analyses, please visit the Zoning and Land Use Assessment webpage. For more information on the data sources and methodology that informed the research findings below, please see APPENDIX: RESEARCH METHODOLOGY . Productive land use This outcome examined the relationship between infrastructure and density citywide. To understand infrastructure access, MPC developed an Urban Services Index, which combined measures to capture the quality of and the proximity to infrastructure across three categories: Transportation, Education, and Neighborhood Amenities. MPC also developed a Density Index based on population density, job density, and the amount of building space compared to developable land. These indices were calculated and assigned to block groups, which were then ranked by quartile. The rankings were used to identify different typologies related to infrastructure access and density (e.g. Low Infrastructure, Moderate Density). Cumulative Urban Services Index Score Infrastructure access and quality are not universal, but each part of the city has infrastructural strengths. While disparities exist in public services across neighborhoods, every part of the city has strengths to support quality of life and continued growth. Using our Urban Services Index, MPC’s analysis indicated that the Northwest and Southwest sides showed strong scores on education infrastructure, the Central and West sides strong scores on transportation infrastructure, and the North and Southeast strong scores on neighborhood amenities. Top-scoring neighborhoods citywide for infrastructure access and quality include The Loop, Edgewater, Uptown, Kenwood, Near South Side, and Hyde Park. Cumulative Density Score There are dense places across the city, but the most dense places are in and near downtown and the North side. While dense areas exist across the city, density—measured through MPC’s Density Index, which captured population, job, and built-space density—is heavily concentrated near the urban core: roughly two-thirds of Chicago's densest areas are located downtown and on the North side. Not only do the Central and North regions contain the city's most dense areas, but the dense areas within these regions also have greater population, job, and built-space density than dense areas located in other regions of the city. Infrastructure-Density Typologies Chicago’s densest areas have a significant amount of low-density zoning. For places in Chicago with the highest levels of infrastructure and density, nearly one-third of land is zoned for low-density residential uses. This compares to 15% of New York City zoned for single family residential, or 0% in Portland. Our areas of existing infrastructural strength offers opportunities to support greater housing supply . A significant portion of the city has more infrastructure than density. Areas classified as Moderate Infrastructure and Low Density comprise nearly 15% of Chicago. These are communities located largely across the West, Southwest, and Southeast sides, which have infrastructure to support more people working, living, and visiting. Gentle increases in density would support growth in these communities. Available groceries and healthcare Zoning does not appear to be responsible for disparities in healthcare and grocery access. Other factors like wealth, census tract demographics, antitrust enforcement, and health insurance access seem to be more related. Though zoning itself may not have caused these problems, there may be an opportunity to use zoning policies or other incentives to encourage the siting of groceries and healthcare in places that lack these key amenities. The wealthiest and most diverse tracts tend to have the best access to primary care, as measured by city-identified primary care clinic locations and self-reported access to doctors. Except for the wealthiest and most diverse tracts, most tracts in Chicago have below the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended density of at least 1 physician practice per 1,000 residents. In 2021, just 20% of Chicago’s population lived in a tract with the WHO-recommended physician density. We also found stark gaps in access to pharmacies and the share of residents with private insurance, with both much more likely on the North side than other parts of the city.. Residents on the North side have greater access to healthy food options. While all census tracts have at least one food store in USDA’s SNAP food vendor database, the North side and parts of the West side are more likely to have food stores likely to provide healthier food options (grocery stories , supermarkets, superstores, etc.) in addition to food stores likely to have less healthy food (convenience stores, drug stores, and dollar stores). Poor grocery access for low-income households is strongly correlated with tract racial demographics, especially segregated Black communities. Northside communities have access to more healthy food stores, and less healthy food stores are evenly distributed Data: USDA SNAP Food Vendors 2025 Food stores overall are most likely to be located in areas zoned B3 . At the same time, the larger food store types—superstores and supermarkets—are most often located within Planned Developments. USDA SNAP vendor counts by zone Note: This excludes specialty stores, pharmacies, corner stores, convenience stores, and farmers markets Source: 2025 USDA SNAP Vendors (grocery stores, supermarkets, and super stores) and 2023 Chicago zoning data Chicago’s zoning ordinance widely allows both medical uses and grocery stores in business-oriented zoning districts, but does not explicitly incentivize these types of development. Medical services is a permitted use in all B and C zones, and all D zones except DR. Food and beverage retail sales is a permitted use in all B and C zones. Other cities use various strategies to incentivize grocery stores in overlay districts (e.g., Tulsa, OK); offer density bonuses to developments that include grocery stores (e.g. Carteret County, NC); or explicitly encourage healthy grocery access (e.g. Madison, WI).

title: Appendix: Research methodology
text: Appendix: Research methodology This section provides an overview of the research design, data sources and preparation, analytical methods, and additional research activities that informed the research findings throughout this report. It is organized into the following subsections: Research scope and process: A brief overview of how the research was designed and conducted and how the research questions across all outcomes were formulated. Data sources and preparation: Documentation of how all of the data used for analysis was collected and processed. Notes on outcome analyses: Documentation of how the research for each outcome was designed and conducted, the research methods employed, and important caveats and limitations that influenced the research findings. Notes on additional analyses: Notes and documentation on additional research activities conducted outside of the longitudinal research detailed in other sections. Research scope and process The research scope was determined collaboratively and iteratively with internal team members and the external Steering Committee, resulting in a list of seven priority outcomes. (See page 6 for more on how outcomes were selected.) For each outcome, findings were grouped into three categories: Understand the outcome: How is this outcome showing up now and how has it shown up over time? For example, for housing affordability, we asked: Is housing affordable for Chicagoans? How does this play out among different populations and in different neighborhoods? Understanding the zoning: What are the zoning and land use policies that we think may affect this outcome? For example, for the same housing affordability focus, we asked: What kind of residential development is allowed under our zoning code? Understanding the relationship: What is the relationship between the zoning and land use policies, and the outcome we see? For example, for housing affordability, we asked: How does zoning impact housing affordability? Findings were shared at regular intervals with Steering Committee members and at public workshops following this format. Each outcome analysis went through several rounds of presentation and iterative feedback with Steering Committee members and public event attendees. Stakeholders reacted to initial findings, provided feedback, and raised additional questions. Where feasible, MPC and Urban Institute team members worked to answer additional questions that were generated during presentations. The findings outlined in this report, while not exhaustive of all the analyses that were conducted, represent key findings generated through this participatory process. Data sources and preparation Longitudinal zoning data The keystone underlying the research findings in the Assessment was a longitudinal zoning dataset we created for Chicago. This dataset allowed us to understand how zoning changes over time may or may not have had an impact on each of the different priority outcomes. To create this dataset, we collected zoning district shapefiles across three years: 2003, 2012, and 2023. We collected the accompanying zoning ordinances for those years so we could quantify bulk and density requirements, use tables, and other relevant zoning information associated with each zoning district and append them to the zoning district shapefiles. We also collected three different land use shapefiles from the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning (CMAP) to understand how actual land uses changed over time, in addition to zoning. Land use data closely, though not perfectly, matched zoning ordinance years: 2001, 2010, and 2020. Zoning and land use variables were used as the primary independent variables across all outcomes. For our analysis of downzoning’s historical impacts, we worked with George Kisiel, whose data on parcels that had been downzoned over the course of several decades was invaluable in enabling us to examine outcomes. ESTABLISHING COMMON GEOGRAPHIES AND UNITS OF ANALYSIS After collecting all zoning and land use variables, we conducted several data transformation steps to prepare variables for analysis. Once prepared, these tract-level zoning variables allowed us to understand the relationships between zoning and all the other tract-level data collected from different secondary sources, such as sociodemographic information collected from the American Community Survey. First, we spatially attributed all zoning and land use variables to the City of Chicago parcel level, using a shapefile of tax parcels from Cook County. This ensured that both zoning and land use variables were transformed into a common geographic unit, but it was also necessary in certain analyses that required parcel-level information (for example, calculating the development envelope, i.e., the maximum amount of housing allowed to be built according to the zoning code). Next, since parcel boundaries change over time, we standardized all zoning and land use data to a common geographical reference point: 2012, the midpoint of our three time periods. The result was a City of Chicago parcel-level longitudinal zoning and land use dataset with zoning and land use data from three points in time that was then used across all outcomes. For census tract-level analyses, 2010 tract boundaries were used as the base geographic unit. Since tract boundaries also change over time, for all data associated with 2000 and 2020 tract boundaries (e.g. 2018 - 2022 ACS data), areal interpolation was used to ensure that all data were standardized into the common 2010 census tract boundary reference point. Parcel-level data was then aggregated to create City of Chicago census tract-level zoning and land use variables to be used in different outcome analyses. Specific independent tract-level variables were created for each outcome. For example, in the Strong Business Corridors outcome analysis, some of the tract-level independent variables related to zoning included the total and percentage of each tract’s total area zoned for different types of Business or Commercial zoning districts. For the Limited Pollution Exposure outcome analysis, we did similar calculations for different types of Manufacturing zoning, industrial land use, and so on. Then variables related to changes in zoning and land use categories were created at the tract level (e.g. the percent of a tract that was rezoned from one zoning district to another). The universe of parcels also somewhat varied, and this was another way the land use data was used in conjunction with zoning data. For instance, in the Affordable Housing outcome analysis, we used the land use data to remove parcels that we considered to be “undevelopable,” e.g. airports, civic landmarks, cemeteries, public parks, and even patches of right-of-way (roads, railroads, highways) that overlap with parcels. THE EXCLUSION OF PLANNED DEVELOPMENTS A major limitation of the zoning data in the study was that the bulk and density requirements and other zoning attributes and all the changes occurring related to Planned Developments—roughly 13% of the City of Chicago’s zoned land—were excluded from our zoning district shapefiles and thus could not be attributed to parcels using the method mentioned above. All information and changes within each Planned Development are described in independent master agreements between the developer and the City of Chicago. Consequently, many of our research findings did not factor in any of these parcels contained within Planned Developments. In our Affordable Housing research, for example, our calculations of zoned capacity were likely significant underestimates in neighborhoods where Planned Developments are more common. In our Strong Business Corridors research, we could not factor in how much business activity and uses were within Planned Developments, and that similarly could potentially skew our research findings. All in all, given that Planned Developments comprise a significant portion of our city’s land area, and our research shows that Planned Developments account for most new multi-family housing units, we understand the importance of addressing these gaps. Analysis of Planned Development agreements for their land uses and the resulting relationships with our key outcomes is a subject for future data work and research. Additional longitudinal variables Simultaneously, we collected data that was used in different outcome-specific analyses. This included socioeconomic and demographic data from the Census American Community Survey (ACS) that were used in all the different outcomes, but also numerous other data sources that varied by outcome. Most of the data collected was at the census tract level, except for a few instances where block group data was necessary, particularly for the accessible public transit hubs and productive land use outcomes. To the extent possible, we attempted to match the data as closely as possible to the years for which we had zoning data. For instance, we used 2018-2022 ACS data to match 2023 zoning, 2010-2014 ACS data to match 2012 zoning, and 2000 Decennial Census data to match 2003 zoning. Perfect year-to-year alignment was not always feasible depending on the source; however, all sources align closely enough to the zoning time periods to serve as proxies, resulting in a dataset with extensive variables representing three distinct time periods. title: Introduction
text: Introduction Nationwide, rising housing costs and a housing shortage are leading policymakers to significantly reform zoning (PDF) to encourage building. At the federal level, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act will give cities and counties new incentives and resources to enable more housing construction. Meanwhile, numerous state governments are developing prohousing land-use legislation, with more than 500 bills introduced in the past year that preempt restrictive local zoning. Regardless of state actions, local policymakers in many cities, such as Chicago, are considering new approaches to spur development and boost affordability. Over the past two years, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s Cut the Tape initiative has explored ways to reform the city’s outdated zoning regulations and streamline approval and review processes. In addition, the city council has updated Chicago’s accessory dwelling unit (ADU) policy twice over the past five years. Recently, it enacted a broader citywide framework that would allow alderpersons to permit ADUs in their wards, though it gave them discretion on some issues, such as whether to require homeowners to live on-site. In this new analysis, we use the Urban Institute’s Housing Market Forecaster to model how several zoning reforms could affect housing development in Chicago by 2041. Specifically, we examine how zoning reforms other cities have made could affect Chicago’s housing supply and distribution across neighborhoods. These reforms include: allowing triplexes to be built in neighborhoods currently zoned exclusively for single-family home construction, legalizing small apartment buildings with four to nine units across the city’s low-density neighborhoods, enabling denser housing developments near transit stations, or combining reforms 2 and 3. We estimate that zoning reforms could enable Chicago to permit up to an additional 9,500 housing units by 2041 above baseline development projections. In addition, we analyze whether changes to the city’s ADU rules—had they been implemented five years ago—could have increased ADU construction compared with what occurred. We find that Chicago could have tripled the number of ADUs permitted between 2021 and 2025 if the city’s rules hadn’t restricted ADU development to five pilot areas and, in some areas, owner-occupied parcels. Taken together, these reforms could help Chicago produce more housing and spread development beyond the Loop and its surroundings, where recent development has been concentrated. But zoning reform alone doesn’t address the market conditions and structural inequities that shape where development occurs—and could even intensify uneven development patterns. To ensure housing growth benefits all residents, the city will need to pair zoning changes with targeted public investment, conscientious private investment, and antidisplacement and community wealth-building measures.

title: Without zoning changes, most housing construction over the next 15 years will likely cluster in downtown Chicago and expensive neighborhoods with higher shares of white residents
text: Without zoning changes, most housing construction over the next 15 years will likely cluster in downtown Chicago and expensive neighborhoods with higher shares of white residents Between 2011 and 2025, Chicago permitted more than 86,400 housing units, most of which were constructed. But this development wasn’t spread evenly across the city . Using a two-stage hurdle regression model to analyze where and how this development occurred, we found that parcels were more likely to have housing permitted on them if they: had accommodating zoning allowances (i.e., they were located in a zoning district that allowed higher development densities); had a higher share of their value come from their land rather than their buildings (i.e., were underbuilt compared with what real estate market actors might consider appropriate); and were located in neighborhoods with lower shares of Black residents, with older average building ages, with lower existing building densities, with higher rent levels, with higher shares of residents commuting by transit, and that were closer to other higher-income neighborhoods. In other words, zoning capacity—what the zoning code allows to be built by right on a parcel—was important but only one of several factors that affected development potential. Land value and neighborhood conditions also strongly influenced development outcomes. The lower probability of housing permitting in areas with a higher share of Black residents reflects systemic racism’s complex influence on developers’ and residents’ perceptions related to neighborhood safety, attractiveness, and profitability rather than any intrinsic characteristic of the communities themselves. Historical practices such as redlining , segregation , discriminatory policing , extractive or predatory lending , and unequal public investment have shaped contemporary housing markets, property values, household wealth, and development financing opportunities in ways that unfortunately continue to influence redevelopment decisions. We used Urban’s Housing Market Forecaster to estimate where housing development permits are most likely to be located over the next 15 years. Without Reforms to the City’s Zoning Code, Permitting Requests from Now Until 2041 Will Likely Be Concentrated In and Around Chicago’s Near Northwest Neighborhoods Estimated probability of a permit for new housing development being requested on a given parcel by 2041, based on the Urban Institute’s Housing Market Forecaster Notes: These estimates assume the city makes no changes to its zoning code and permits continue at the same pace as they did from 2011 to 2025 under the same economic conditions. Estimates are for cumulative development from 2026 to 2041. Sources: Authors’ analysis of Cook County Assessor parcel data, City of Chicago zoning data, and 2020–24 census tract–level American Community Survey data. The probability that a parcel will have residential permitting by 2041 is highest in neighborhoods north and northwest of downtown. In comparison, we estimate that parcels located in neighborhoods on the far south, southwest, and western areas of the city have the lowest probabilities of residential permitting. Neighborhoods on much of the far west side would have limited housing development probabilities, as well. However, permit probabilities are not the same as estimated housing units. A permit may be for a single-family home or a several-hundred-unit apartment tower. If the city makes no changes to its zoning code, permits continue at the same pace as they did from 2011 to 2025, and economic conditions remain similar to today’s, we estimate that Chicago would permit another 87,500 housing units on parcels where housing can be built by right. Most of these units would be in central Chicago. Permitting probabilities for downtown parcels are low, but the average project located there is much larger, so our model estimates most new housing will be built downtown. Under Chicago’s Current Zoning, Most Housing Units Permitted Between Now and 2041 Will Likely Be Concentrated In and Around the City’s Downtown Estimated housing unit permits per ward by 2041, based on the Urban Institute’s Housing Market Forecaster Notes: These estimates assume the city makes no changes to its zoning code and permits continue at the same pace as they did from 2011 to 2025 under the same economic conditions. Estimates are for cumulative development from 2026 to 2041. Sources: Authors’ analysis of Cook County Assessor parcel data, City of Chicago zoning data, and 2020–24 census tract–level American Community Survey data. These are modeled estimates, not guarantees of future development. Developers’ economic calculations, value assessments, and developers’ and residents’ perceptions of neighborhood conditions could change between now and 2041. Additionally, the city, private actors, or community groups could invest in infrastructure, amenities, and marketing that changes neighborhoods’ perceived value. Still, these estimates show how permitting and development patterns could be distributed without significant policy or investment intervention.

title: Legalizing small-scale apartment buildings and upzoning around transit stations could add 5 to 11 percent more housing, compared with the baseline, by 2041
text: Legalizing small-scale apartment buildings and upzoning around transit stations could add 5 to 11 percent more housing, compared with the baseline, by 2041 To understand how policymakers in Chicago could boost housing supply and affordability, we use Urban’s Housing Market Forecaster to see how zoning reforms in other cities (such as Boston, Massachusetts; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Portland, Oregon; and Seattle, Washington) could affect Chicago’s housing development. We examine the effects of: allowing duplexes and triplexes on parcels that are currently exclusively zoned for single-family residential construction; small apartment buildings (four to nine units) on parcels that are currently exclusively zoned for single-family residential construction; enabling higher-density multifamily buildings within one-quarter mile of an L, Metra, or frequent Chicago Transit Authority bus station; and combining reforms 2 and 3. Notes: Estimated effect is only for parcels where residential uses are allowed by right. The model does not include potential planned developments. For reform 1, we assume triplexes are allowed only on lots with at least 2,500 square feet; we also increase the allowed floor area ratio to 1.05. For reform 2, we allow more units on larger parcels (scaling up as the parcel size grows) and increase the allowed floor area ratio to 1.25. For reform 3, we assume that parcel areas that could be affected by this change could be as small as 1,650 square feet, and that the allowed floor area ratio is increased to 2.5. Reform 2 fully encompasses reform 1, in that it would also allow duplexes or triplexes if the lot is too small to allow bigger projects. We estimate that allowing triplexes by right on small lots would increase the number of units permitted by 5,900. Allowing four-to-nine-unit buildings on medium and large lots would add 8,100 permitted units. Allowing high-density housing throughout areas near transit would add 4,100 units. Combined, the latter two reforms would add 9,500 units above the baseline forecast. Given the city’s current estimated current gap of 226,000 affordable homes , these reforms would not fully address the city’s housing needs, but they represent a start. Combining transit-oriented and small-scale apartment development could help the city meet the housing needs of a wider range of residents and neighborhoods. Finally, we mapped where each reform would add new units. We estimate that reforms 1 and 2, which are designed to incentivize additional smaller-scale apartment buildings, would likely increase housing permits in the far northwest and southwest of the city over the next 15 years. Notably, residents in these neighborhoods have on average substantially higher incomes than those in the far south side of the city. We estimate that allowing denser housing in transit areas (reform 3) would have the greatest effect on Jefferson Park, Lincoln Square, and Portage Park. As expected, reform 4 would combine the relative impacts of reforms 2 and 3 on different areas. Across all four reforms, we estimate that housing permitting in the near and far southeast would be noticeably lower than in other areas of the city: under 100 additional units per ward compared with 400 to 1,250 more in other neighborhoods. These results suggest that without intentional intervention and investment to balance housing production, zoning reforms could perpetuate—or exacerbate—housing inequities.

title: Expanding the ADU pilot citywide could have led to 3.5 times as many ADU permits between 2021 and 2025
text: Expanding the ADU pilot citywide could have led to 3.5 times as many ADU permits between 2021 and 2025 ADUs offer cities a fast and generally popular way to add housing with proven results . In 2021, Chicago launched a pilot initiative that allowed construction of detached or integrated ADUs in five different neighborhoods. In three of these areas, the city required owners to live in the primary house or unit on the lot to qualify to build an ADU. In 2026, the pilot became opt-in citywide, with alderpersons choosing what restrictions they wish to place on ADU development terms. To help city leaders and alderpersons weigh how their decisions could affect housing production levels, we analyzed how the pilot’s original geographic and owner-occupancy restrictions affected development levels. Using a new housing forecast (logit regression) model, we explored what housing and lot characteristics were associated with ADU development. Between 2021 and 2025, property owners permitted 343 ADUs in the pilot areas. Among these units: 28 percent were above-garage coach or carriage houses, built on lots with 2.8 existing units on average, 66 percent were internal conversions (e.g., basement, attic, or other space conversions to add units), built on lots with 4.6 existing units on average, and the remaining 6 percent were either external additions (built on lots with 2.2 units existing units on average), legalization of existing ADUs, or other forms that were unclear from their permit application. Overall, the pilot’s permitted ADUs largely represented additional units within, attached to, or outside of existing small multifamily buildings across the city. Our model shows that across the pilot areas, ADUs were more likely to be permitted on lots in places with high demand for housing and land, and that also had higher amounts of unbuilt land on the parcel. ADUs were more common on parcels in neighborhoods with higher housing values, more multifamily housing, and no owner-occupancy requirement under the initiative. In addition, ADU construction was more likely if a parcel had a greater building value and lower land value. Notably, this is the opposite of what we found for regular housing permits between 2011 and 2025, indicating that ADU reforms are complementary to rather than substitutions for missing middle and transit-oriented housing reforms. We then estimated how ADU permitting could have changed had the city removed the owner-occupancy rules in some of the city’s pilot areas. We found this change could have increased the number of permitted ADUs by about 30 percent, resulting in about 100 additional units between 2021 and 2025. If the pilot had allowed ADUs to be built throughout Chicago, without any owner-occupancy rules, we estimate that the city could have permitted about 860 additional ADUs over the four years for a total of 1,203 ADUS —or 3.5 times the number of ADUs that were actually permitted. They could also consider ADU caps or quotas per ward, rather than the current opt-in structure.

title: Zoning reforms can help boost housing supply, but other investments are needed to ensure development is spread fairly across the city
text: Zoning reforms can help boost housing supply, but other investments are needed to ensure development is spread fairly across the city By-right zoning changes for small-scale apartments and transit-oriented density, plus an expanded ADU policy could meaningfully increase housing permitting in Chicago. According to our model, the city could permit about 97,000 housing units by 2041 (87,500 from baseline development estimates plus 9,500 from the combined zoning reforms) and potentially add thousands more units by liberalizing the city’s new ADU policy. But intentional investment is needed to spread development across the city without displacing residents. Our analysis highlights that zoning reforms alone risk concentrating development in already-advantaged neighborhoods and exacerbating the city’s already polarized investment landscape. To boost housing development across the city, the city council should combine regulatory liberalization with targeted public investment and antidisplacement measures. To spur housing and economic development in neighborhoods that aren’t expected to have much development in the coming years, city leaders could invest in predevelopment work to clean and green vacant lots , offer property tax adjustments, expand homeownership and wealth-building programs , strengthen community land trusts , or strengthen local investment programs to build wealth among current residents .

title: ABOUT THE DATA
text: ABOUT THE DATA This analysis combines parcel-level data from the Cook County Assessor, the City of Chicago, and our research partners at the Chicago Metropolitan Planning Council—including panel zoning data, building permits, building footprints, and transit access—with census tract characteristics from the American Community Survey. To analyze housing development from 2011 to 2025, we examine parcels where residential development was allowed by right. We estimate each parcel’s zoned housing capacity and use a two-stage Poisson hurdle regression model. For parcels that underwent planned development reforms (i.e., a custom site plan that bypasses zoning requirements through negotiations with the city) in this timeframe, we assume that by-right development is equivalent to each planned development’s final underlying zoning district (as available). Between 2006 and 2024, more than 60 percent of all multifamily development was in planned developments. Our approach is limited because we do not have data on all planned development projects and thus exclude about half of these projects from our analysis. This also means a large share of the by-right permits we evaluate are on parcels that underwent planned development changes in the past. Using this data, we estimate the likelihood that a parcel received a housing permit based on its zoning, land value, and neighborhood characteristics. Then, we estimate the number of units permitted on parcels where development occurred. We applied these relationships to 2026 parcel and neighborhood conditions to construct a 2041 baseline and then model how permitting could change under four zoning reforms that would allow triplexes, four-to-nine-unit buildings, and higher-density housing near frequent transit. We assume that the baseline level of development in the next 15 years is the same as that over the past 15 years. For the ADU analysis, we link ADU permits issued from 2021 to 2025 to parcel and neighborhood characteristics and estimate a logistic regression for eligible parcels in Chicago’s pilot areas. We then sum parcel-level predicted probabilities and the geographic variation across pilot areas that did and didn’t require owner occupancy to estimate how many ADUs might have been permitted without the owner-occupancy requirements. Finally, we apply the model to eligible low-density residential parcels outside the pilot areas to simulate a citywide program. These scenarios illustrate how permitting might differ under alternative policies. They remain sensitive to future market and demographic conditions.
